item.title: [BBC World] US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Donald Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his party to end the warBySareen Habeshian and David GrittenPublished3 November 2026, 03:39 GMTUpdated 1 minute ago
The US has carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing on a US aircraft.
Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The US military has not commented on the strikes, which came as mediators stepped up their efforts to prevent a return to all-out war after the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Earlier on Monday, the president told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.
"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."
He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.
There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".

India lifted nearly 500 million out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, with extreme poverty dropping from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent in the world’s most populous nation during the same period, according to a new report by the World Bank.
The only other parallel in poverty reduction on this scale is China, which lifted more than 800 million people out of extreme poverty — though that was over a period of 40 years.

item.description:
The U.S. will mediate working-level talks between Ukrainian and Russian officials in November, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Tuesday night. In a post on X, Witkoff said the discussions on Nov. 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi would "focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."
He added that American negotiators would meet this week with representatives from European allies and the NATO alliance, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, to discuss future security guarantees for Ukraine, which has been one of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recurring demands for any deal with Russia.
"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin shakes hands with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff at Constantine Palace in St. Petersburg, Russia, Oct. 21, 2026.
Sputnik/Kristina Solovyova/Pool via Reuters
Ukraine and Russia have held several rounds of talks mediated by the U.S. during President Trump's second term, often yielding prisoner exchanges or other low-level agreements, but Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite some controversial concessions from the Trump administration, has thus far refused to drop his demand for Ukraine to accept Russia's unilateral annexation of some territory siezed over the course of the grueling war.
Zelenskyy, likewise, has consistently ruled out accepting Russia's seizure of territory by force, and many U.S. allies in Europe agree that legitimizing Putin's landgrab would set a dangerous precedent.

item.title: [NPR News] Review: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is superb, streamlined and safe
item.description:
Video Game Reviews
Review: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is superb, streamlined and safe
November 3, 20266:00 AM ET
James Perkins Mastromarino
Link, the Hero of Time, grown-up and newly awoken from a magical seven-year slumber.
Nintendo
hide caption
toggle caption i
Nintendo
With its tale of an idyllic world despoiled by the lust for power, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time feels as relevant today as it did in 1998. Nintendo's new remake, out Thursday on the Switch 2, enshrines its place in the gaming canon for generations to come. But despite its stupendous production values and painstaking details, the game left me feeling oddly bereft.
Perhaps I should have expected as much. Ocarina of Time weaponizes nostalgia even within its narrative, as the protagonist Link ventures to save his post-apocalyptic world as an adult after first working through it as a kid. You'll uncover old characters enduring new catastrophes. You'll try to rescue everyone you meet. You'll strive to bring things back to how they were before — no, better than they were before.
Seven years stretch between Link's childhood and adult adventures. 28 years yawn between the remake and the original's release. Both in and out of the game, Ocarina of Time makes us yearn for an idealized past...

WASHINGTON -- The United States has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, a U.S. official said Monday, on the eve of crucial midterm elections.
Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island. The official, who wasn’t authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said that “Iranians using surface to air missiles against U.S. assets” had been targeted.
The strikes appeared to be limited as opposed to a return to full hostilities but followed President Donald Trump previously saying the U.S. would not launch new strikes on Iran before Tuesday's midterms. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress.
The region is on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran, and the new strikes, which were reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal, are certain to raise fresh concerns. Backchannel negotiations also are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the more than 8-month-old war that’s rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran.
The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September, but thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers hauling Iranian oil from getting to the global market. item.title: [CBS News World] U.S. launches defensive strikes at Iranian targets
item.description:
The U.S. military has launched limited defensive strikes at Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz, three U.S. officials confirmed to CBS News.
A senior U.S. official said the strikes targeted Iran's Qeshm Island after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired at an American aircraft.
The Wall Street Journal first reported on the strikes on Monday.
The strikes came on the eve of Election Day, as President Trump floats restarting hostilities with Iran after the midterms and as the U.S. and Qatari mediators broker talks on a U.S.-Iran deal.
As the war enters its ninth month, Mr. Trump's rhetoric has continued to swing back and forth between striking a deal and launching sustained strikes against Iran again.
In a Truth Social post earlier Monday, the president said a deal "could happen" and that "Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible." Later that night, in an appearance on Fox News, Mr. Trump said "we still have to take care of" several sites in Iran, including Pickaxe Mountain, which houses a suspected nuclear site. During his appearance on Sean Hannity's program, Mr. Trump said it was "not a big deal" and could be done in "an hour."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a weekend call with Mr. Trump, pushed for further sustained strikes against Iran, according to The Associated Press. Mr. Trump acknowledged the call had taken place, saying he had a "very good talk with him," but did not elaborate on what he and Netanyahu discussed.
The war has loomed large over both the U.S. midterm and Israeli parliamentary elections. In the U.S., rising costs stemming from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have led to cratering support for Mr. Trump and the Republican Party.
In Israel, Netanyahu's party lost its majority in the first parliamentary elections since Oct. 7, 2023.
As of mid-October, the Iran war had cost the U.S. military at least $47.1 billion, according to a new estimate from U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News...

item.title: [BBC World] Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesBySareen HabeshianReporting fromLos AngelesPublished8 hours ago
The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count.
The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state.
Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate.
The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term.
The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction.
"The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.
Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots.
California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.

Police in South Africa have arrested five suspects connected to a violent farm robberyByThe Associated PressNovember 2, 2026, 12:00 PM
Share
JOHANNESBURG -- Police in South Africa have arrested five suspects in connection with a violent farm robbery in the North West province in which a 50-year-old farmer was shot and had his ears cut off.
The suspects, aged 26 to 56, are expected to appear before the Ventersdorp magistrates’ court on Tuesday on charges of house robbery, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition, Col. Adele Mybrugh said Monday.
Police initially arrested two suspects before detaining three more on Sunday near Potchefstroom, about 120 kilometers (74 miles) west-southwest of Johannesburg. Officers seized four firearms, two of which were linked to the attack, along with clothing and jewelry.
The attack occurred Oct. 28 on a farm in Syferfontein, near Ventersdorp, in North West province. Three armed men wearing balaclavas confronted a farmworker mowing the lawn, demanded to know where the owner was, and bound his hands and feet with cable ties, police said.
When the farmer arrived, the attackers shot him in the upper body, dragged him inside, bound him and stabbed and assaulted him. They stole three firearms from a safe and fled in his pickup truck, police said.
The worker freed himself and called for help. The farmer was hospitalized in serious condition.
The Moral Regeneration Movement, a civil society organization, identified the farmer as Donovan Marx and said Monday that he was recovering in the hospital.

item.title: [ABC News World] Britain says many migrants will have to wait longer to win the right to stay
item.description:
Britain says many migrants will have to wait longer to win the right to stay
The British government says it will double the wait time for many immigrants to settle permanently, although key workers and higher earners will be exemptedByJILL LAWLESS Associated PressNovember 2, 2026, 12:22 PM
Share
LONDON -- The British government announced Monday that it will double the time many immigrants must wait before they can settle permanently in the country, though it exempted key workers and high earners from the changes.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said people who come to the U.K. on work visas will have to wait a decade to be granted permanent residency status, which carries the right to work, study, access free health care and claim benefits. But a higher income can speed up the process. People who earn at least 50,000 pounds ($67,000) a year will only have to wait five years, as will public-sector workers including doctors, nurses and teachers. Immigrants on salaries above 125,000 pounds a year can apply for settlement after three years.
Mahmood said the changes will be introduced during 2027 and will restore fairness to the immigration system by linking the right to settle to an immigrant’s contribution to Britain.
She told lawmakers that her own parents came to the U.K. from Pakistan half a century ago “because they knew we do things differently here, and that we value above all else fair play. It is my responsibility to ensure our migration system lives up to that ideal.”
The changes are a softening of proposals Mahmood made last year which drew opposition from some in the governing Labour Party. The original plan would have made lower-paid immigrant workers, including those who keep Britain’s care homes running, wait 15 years to settle permanently. Care workers will continue to be eligible for settlement after five years, as long as they earn at least 25,000 pounds a year.
The median U.K. salary is about 39,000 pounds a year.

item.title: [Guardian China] Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer: the Amazonian town transformed by a rampant mining boom
item.description:
Chang Yuequan with a photo of the gold haul from one of his mines the previous day worth £20,000 Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The Guardian
View image in fullscreen
Chang Yuequan with a photo of the gold haul from one of his mines the previous day worth £20,000 Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The Guardian
Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer: the Amazonian town transformed by a rampant mining boom
Mayaya, once-remote, has become a hub for Chinese companies. But critics accuse them of exploitation and illegal exports
The pork belly hits the oil with a sizzle, and a rich aroma of soy sauce and caramelising sugar fills the kitchen. Zhang Changchun, a middle-aged man from China’s Heilongjiang province, is cooking dinner for his friends on a warm evening in Mayaya, a small town in the Bolivian Amazon.
“Bolivia is my happy place,” he says in Mandarin as he adds the dish to a table overflowing with pork trotters, duck wings and braised sábalo fish. In this small restaurant, a group of half a dozen Chinese men gathers most nights to eat, drink and play mahjong.
View image in fullscreen
Zhang Changchun, a Chinese chef and mine investor, at dinner in Mayaya, Bolivia. Photograph: Benjamin Swift/The Guardian
Each man plays a critical role in the town’s booming gold business. Some work as investors or miners; others import supplies and equipment. Together, they run most of the town’s mining operations: about 20 open-pit mines and 12 dredge boats, operated by about 2,000 Bolivian and 200 Chinese workers.
The table gets rowdy as the men debate their afternoon games over high-end Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer. Almost every conversation revolves around money.
In less than a decade, private Chinese mining companies have turned this once-remote Amazonian town into a hub of gold speculation. Mining equipment stores, hotels and Chinese restaurants now line the main street.

item.title: [Guardian China] UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn
item.description:
Keir Starmer visited China in January, the first trip by a British prime minister since Theresa May travelled there in 2018. Photograph: Carl Court/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
Keir Starmer visited China in January, the first trip by a British prime minister since Theresa May travelled there in 2018. Photograph: Carl Court/Reuters
UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn
Commons committee says lack of coherent strategy is hampering business and leaving national security risks unaddressed
The UK is making up policy on China “as it goes along” and risks having its strategy dictated by Washington or Beijing, a parliamentary report has concluded.
An investigation by the Commons business, innovation, science and trade select committee said Labour’s failure to formulate a coherent strategy since 2024 “combined the worst of both worlds” for the UK in relation to China.
Liam Byrne, Labour MP and chair of the committee said the UK’s policy on China meant it was also endangering its business with the EU with the risk of being “cut off” from big manufacuring contracts.
The government could neither deliver commercial opportunities to British businesses nor control the “increasing exposure to unquantified, managed risk” in relations with China, it found.
The report said: “In 2024, the new government promised a strategic, long-term, consistent UK approach to China. It has not delivered on this.
“Britain must shape its own relationship with China or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.”
The UK’s relationship with China has been marked by a lack of engagement in the last 10 years, with Keir Starmer making the first official visit in January since Theresa May in 2018.

item.title: [Guardian China] The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading
item.description:
Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September 2026. Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesAnalysis
The US-China trade war seems to have subsided – but the sense of calm is misleading Eduardo Porter
A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities
Donald Trump’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the Federal Reserve cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.
The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.
The truce reached by Washington and Beijing last year in their escalating trade conflict, which has been extended until next January, lowered the heat between the two – putting an end to the escalation of tit-for-tat tariffs and opening a door to some as yet undefined future trade deal.
But neither China nor the US has done anything to establish the mutual assurances that could limit the outbreak of new hostilities. Rather, they are both focused on gaining the upper hand in what seems like an inevitable next round, in a standoff that both sides have defined as a national security priority, essential to ensure economic, technological and military supremacy.

item.title: [BBC China] Crypto giant Binance hit by $6.3bn hack suspected to be largest in history
item.description:
Image source, VCG/VCG via Getty ImagesByOsmond Chia, Business reporter and Angus ThompsonPublished30 October 2026
Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that $6.3bn (£4.7bn) of digital assets have been impacted by what is thought to be the biggest crypto hack on record.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said about half of those assets had been frozen but that many remained in the hands of the hackers, adding that it will "cover all losses".
The firm said while initial checks suggested an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals, "our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach".
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident, which eclipses a record-setting $1.5bn hack on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor.
Cyber-security firm Check Point said the unit is also known in the industry as Lazarus Group, which has been blamed for the 2025 hack.
Check Point's chief information security officer Jayant Dave said the losses estimated by Binance made it "the largest crypto theft on record".
AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report that several elements of the Binance attack resemble earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
The lab's global head of policy Ari Redbord told the BBC the Binance hack is a "watershed moment" that is unlike anything the industry has seen.
The attacker still holds an enormous sum of stolen assets, meaning efforts to trace and recover the funds are far from over, Redbord added.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it has more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
The exchange has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.

item.title: [Guardian World] Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
item.description:
Wemmer Pan Road, near Rosettenville in Johannesburg, has been occupied by illegal gold miners. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian
There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffectiveBy Rachel Savage in Durban Deep
Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.
In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).
Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.
“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.
View image in fullscreen
Cora Bailey, who founded the charity Claw, has encountered illegal miners since 1991. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian
Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.
South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

item.title: [Guardian World] Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
item.description:
Nusseibeh said she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE to be ‘mindful of the obligations of independence’ the UN role would entail. Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
Nusseibeh said she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE to be ‘mindful of the obligations of independence’ the UN role would entail. Photograph: David Dee Delgado/Reuters
Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.
Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.
The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.

item.title: [BBC China] China made Mbappé apologise - but many don't know exactly what he said
item.description:
Image source, CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty ImagesByFan WangPublished29 October 2026
On Monday night, as Kylian Mbappé was attending the Ballon d'Or ceremony in London, he was also becoming the centre of a huge controversy on Chinese social media.
Football fans had stumbled upon a clip of him joking about the meme that makes him "laugh the most" - where his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao Zedong, who oversaw one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past.
The controversy spread like wildfire as Chinese brands cut him off one by one and China Media Group, the parent group of state broadcaster CCTV, suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches. A foreign ministry spokesperson said: "Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."
But on the Chinese internet, few were explicitly spelling out those words and actions, or even using the name of Mao - who remains a near-sacred figure in the country.

China's sophisticated censorship system, which cuts 1.4 billion people off from the global internet, meant many didn't know exactly what had happened.
The accusation of "hurting the feelings of the Chinese people" alone seemed enough to trigger a tsunami of anger, amplified by social media algorithms and a heavily controlled internet, where people are wary of disagreeing with the majority view.
It wasn't long before Mbappé, one of the biggest football stars in the world, said he was "sincerely sorry" for his "ill-judged" comment. His club, Real Madrid, and the Spanish league La Liga, also issued apologies. China is a huge market for the world's most popular sport.

item.title: [BBC China] Hong Kong's leader apologises for deadly high-rise fire
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
John Lee (centre) bowed in apology along with top officialsByTessa WongPublished29 October 2026
The chief executive of Hong Kong, John Lee, has apologised for a massive fire that ripped through an apartment complex last year and killed 168 people.
Speaking at a press conference, Lee promised major reforms to government departments to ensure such an incident would not happen again.
A report by an independent committee, released by the government at the press conference, found that the fire was caused by "misconduct" by the private sector as well as "decades of failure" by government bodies.
The massive blaze at Wang Fuk Court in November 2025 was the deadliest the city had seen in decades. Dozens of people have been arrested on suspicion of manslaughter, fraud or corruption.
At the start of the press conference on Thursday, John Lee said he was "deeply sorrowful" about the fire and that on behalf of his government, "I apologise to the victims as well as the city's residents".
He then stood up and bowed, along with several top officials.
Later he announced that the city's housing secretary Winnie Ho had resigned to take accountability for the fire.
The independent committee's report found that the fire was most likely caused by a "glowing source, likely a cigarette" which ignited "paper materials" at the apartment complex, which was undergoing extensive renovation at the time.
Officials have said the government may start using AI and drones with infra-red cameras to detect and identify smokers on construction sites.
The report also found that the construction companies in charge of the renovation used sub-standard building materials and had unsafe procedures.
This included using scaffolding nets that were not fire retardant and covering up windows with inflammable foam boards for a prolonged period of time.

item.title: [Guardian World] Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
item.description:
Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, pictured in 2017. Photograph: Roger Anis/AP
View image in fullscreen
Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, pictured in 2017. Photograph: Roger Anis/AP
Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.
Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.
According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.
“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.
Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.The news website that’s keeping press freedom alive in Egypt | Leslie T Chang
Read more
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.
